title: Async in Practice: Building a Writing Culture

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Welcome back to Work Reimagined. I’m Sarah Johnson. A few episodes ago, Mark Rivera told us remote work is really about async-first culture and documentation. Today we’re testing that idea in practice.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Thanks for having me, Sarah. I run operations at Fieldnote, a 60-person fully distributed company, so I live this every day.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Mark pointed to GitLab and Automattic and their handbooks. Is a handbook really where you start?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Honestly, no. A handbook is the output. The starting point is a writing habit. If people don’t write decisions down day to day, a handbook just becomes a graveyard of stale pages.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: So what does a writing habit look like concretely?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: We use short decision memos: the problem, the options, the recommendation, and who decides. Anything that affects more than one team gets a memo before it gets a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Does that slow things down?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: At first, yes. Our first quarter, decisions took about a day longer. By the second quarter we had cut recurring meetings by roughly 40 percent, and new hires were ramping in three weeks instead of six.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: That onboarding number is striking.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: It’s the biggest win. A new hire can read the last six months of memos and understand why things are the way they are, not just what they are.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: What goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Two things. Documentation rot, where nobody owns updating pages, and writing anxiety. Not everyone is comfortable writing, especially non-native English speakers. We had to make it clear that clarity beats polish.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: How do you fight documentation rot?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Every page has a named owner and a review date. If the review date passes, the page gets flagged as possibly outdated. It’s simple, but it works.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Time for our listener question. Jordan from Toronto asks: our team says it’s async, but Slack still expects replies in minutes. How do we fix that?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Publish explicit response-time norms. For us, Slack is a same-day medium, not a same-minute one. Urgent things get a phone call. Once leaders model it, the team follows.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Mark predicted async would become standard practice. Do you agree?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Mostly, but I’d add a nuance. Async will become standard for decisions and status updates. Sync time won’t disappear; it’ll get reserved for conflict, creativity, and relationships.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: One piece of advice for a team starting today?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Pick one recurring meeting and replace it with a written update for a month. Measure what you lose and what you gain.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Great challenge. Thanks Hannah, and thanks to everyone listening to Work Reimagined. Next time, we’re talking about how managers actually measure performance remotely.
